newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain swallows EU beef label deal.
newsitem.headline: Britain swallows EU beef label deal.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday swallowed a European Union deal under which beef sold in shops will from January 2000 have to carry a label showing where it comes from, although this could make exports difficult.

Britain and Italy had for three days blocked a unanimous agreement but were eventually won over by a face-saving concession from the Dutch EU Presidency allowing them to opt out from compulsory labelling for beef sold on its territory.
"I think it's good for consumers and for the public at large," Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen told a news conference after the marathon meeting.

EU farm ministers were under considerable pressure to improve food safety after a damning European Commission report revealed widespread failure among EU member states to detect and eradicate the fatal cattle brain disease bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
"The BSE crisis has shown how important a good identification and registration system is to prevent the spread of animal diseases," Van Aartsen said in a statement.
British officials put a brave face on the deal in the absence of agriculture minister Douglas Hogg who flew back to London on Monday.
"We got what we wanted," one official said, referring to the opt-out clause and more flexibility on data reporting deadlines.

Unanimity was required after ministers rejected a European Commission proposal that would have given the European Parliament power to decide jointly the creation of EU cattle identification and beef labelling systems.
An angry EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler criticised farm ministers for snubbing the parliament which now only has an advisory role.
"I regret very much that by proceeding in this way, the prliament's participation was curtailed," he said. "Members of the parliament are representatives of the people and are elected by them."
In defiant mood, the burly Austrian farm commissioner warned ministers that in future he would propose wherever possible that the parliament be given joint decision-making power.

The agreement fixes a framework for beef labelling until the end of 1999, allowing those member states who wish to do so to introduce voluntary schemes from July 1, 1997 with labels showing at least a cattle identification number.
Germany, Austria and France are among countries expected to press ahead with labelling schemes but they will not be able to block imports of unlabelled beef before 2000.
Farm ministers are due to decide by the end of 1999 whether extra information should be put on beef labels and whether other meat products should be labelled.
Labelling of beef imports from countries outside the EU would be subject to negotiation and would have to respect World Trade Organisation free trade rules.
Regarding cattle identification, eartags and passports will be compulsory from January 1998 and computerised data bases from 2000. EU funding would be available for the computerisation.
Britain had been worried that indicating where cattle were born, raised and slaughtered would deter continental buyers and infringe trade in the single EU market.
Italy, which imports a lot of calves from eastern Europe, was concerned that providing such information would create an adverse reaction among Italian consumers.
